In Wren’s room. When we brought her things up. A small book. With diagrams. I don’t suppose I could go up and look for it? And wait for her up there?” “Go on up,” said Mrs Pellow, without a flicker. “First door. Mind the stair, the third one’s loose. I’ll bring you a cup of tea.” That is the trouble with lying to kind people. It is so very easy. The little bedroom was under the roof, with a sloping ceiling and a narrow bed with a patchwork quilt, every square of it white in the light from the window. Tobin, in the doorway, suddenly saw Wren lying there under it, curled up small, the way she curled up by the fire in Ash’s tower. He saw it so clearly that he nearly said her name. There was nobody there. Mrs Pellow came puffing up behind him with the tea, and set it on the windowsill, and patted his arm, and went down again. Tobin stood and looked at the cup until it stopped steaming. Beside the bed stood a small table with a drawer. The drawer was shut. But round the crack at the top of it, so faint that you would only have seen it if you knew to look, there was a thread of gold. Tobin knelt down in front of it, and said his reasons over to himself, quickly, the way you say a lesson you are afraid of forgetting. She put it away. She doesn’t even look at it. She’s going to stay here and be a Pellow and never go anywhere again. And technically it’s only a brass container with a flame in it, and my father is a person. He said he was sorry. He’s never said sorry to me in my whole life. He pulled the drawer open. The lamp lay on a folded handkerchief: small and battered and dented, with its hairline crack in the glass and its little hook on top. Its flame was lower than he had ever seen it, a quiet, patient bead of gold, like an eye half closed. Where its light touched the plain white wood, the wood went warm brown, the colour of a nut. Tobin reached in and picked it up. It was hot. Not warm. Not the warmth he remembered from the Black Stair, when Wren had put it in his hands and it had sat there like a living thing, glad to be carried. This was the heat of a kettle-handle left on the stove. It went into his fingers and up through his palms in one hard, bright, astonishing sting. He gasped and nearly dropped it. He knew what it meant. He was not stupid, whatever else he was. He had heard Wren tell the story a dozen times, with relish: Silas Grubb reaching for it with his twenty silver crowns, and jumping back yelping. It burns the hand of anyone who tries to buy or sell it. Tobin had written that down in his notebook once, under a heading. He had found it very interesting at the time, as a principle. He was not buying it. He was not selling it. He was — trading it. For a person. That was different. The lamp did not think it was different. Tobin knelt on Wren’s floor with tears of pain standing in his eyes, and the lamp burning in his hands. For one long moment he very nearly put it back. He wanted that remembered, afterwards: that he very nearly did. Then he thought of his father’s hand, writing I was wrong. He pulled off his coat and wrapped the lamp in it, round and round, as tight as he could, and pushed the drawer shut with his elbow, and went down the stairs. “Find it, pet?” called Mrs Pellow. “Yes,” said Tobin. “Thank you.” “You’ll catch your death without your coat on!” “It’s not cold,” said Tobin, which was a strange thing to say in Vaelport, where it was always cold; and he went out of the white door and down Lantern Steps without looking back. He was afraid that if he looked back, he would see the door blue. He went back by the Salt Lantern first. He had not meant to; his feet took him there. The landlady looked up from her counter as he came in with the coat bundled against his chest, and said, “Aren’t you cold, sir?” and he went past her and up the four flights as if he had not heard. In the empty room he took his mother’s compass out of his pocket and opened the lid. Home is where the light is. The needle swung, and shivered, and settled: north and a bit east. Away from the lighthouse, and the sea, and everything in Vaelport. Pointing, as steady as a finger, the other way. “It’s not fair,” he whispered to it. “You don’t know. He’s in a cell.” The needle did not move. He could not carry it. That was the plain fact. He could not do what he meant to do with that thing in his pocket, pointing the other way the whole time. He shut the lid, gently, and laid the compass on his pillow. Then he went down the stairs again, quickly, before he could pick it up. At the end of the long white harbour wall the lighthouse stood on its rock, and its great glowstone shone out over the water, where there were no ships for it to warn, and back over the city, where there was no dark for it to drive away. Varrick had said any hour, any day. Tobin did not wait for a better one. The heat came through every fold of the coat, however tightly he held it, as if he were carrying a loaf straight out of the oven. He shifted it from arm to arm. It made no difference. The lamp knew exactly where he was taking it. Halfway along the wall a man sat on an upturned crate, mending a crab-pot. His flat tired eyes followed Tobin a little way. “Here,” he said. “Aren’t you one of that old lamp-man’s lot? The mad one with the sticks, that they took up out of the square.” Tobin did not stop walking. “I don’t know him,” he said. He said it quite loudly and quite clearly, and it was not even a little bit true. The man shrugged and went back to his crab-pot. And Tobin walked on with the lamp burning against his ribs, and found that he was crying, not loudly, just steadily, the tears running down under his spectacles into his collar. He told himself it was the pain in his hands. Some of it was. It’s for Father, he said to himself, in time with his feet. It’s for Father. It’s for Father. It is a strange thing, but the more times you say a thing like that, the less it sounds like a reason, and the more it sounds like a noise. He put his hand to his throat, and held the pendant, and went on. The door at the foot of the lighthouse was open. The stair wound up and up round the inside of the white wall, two hundred and twelve steps; and at the top was the round glass room under the great glowstone, with the narrow iron gallery outside it. A door in the glass stood open. The wind came in off the sea and went round and round. Far below, the water broke white on the rock. Captain Varrick was already there. He stood out on the gallery at the rail with his back to the stair, looking out to sea, as if he had been standing there for hours and would happily stand for hours more. He did not turn round when Tobin came up the last step. He only said, pleasantly, “Today, then. I thought it might be.” Then he turned, and looked at Tobin’s wet face and the bundled coat held out stiff in two shaking hands; and something in his own face settled, very slightly, the way a man sits back when a long game of cards comes out exactly as he expected. “Well,” he said. “Let us see it.” Tobin unwrapped the coat with fingers that would hardly obey him. In the great white glare from overhead, the lamp looked small and dull and yellow, like a brass button dropped in snow. But its little flame was still burning; and it was still, Tobin could feel, every bit as hot. “My father,” he said. His voice cracked in the middle. “You said if I brought it, he’d go free. You said she keeps her bargains.” “I did say that,” agreed Varrick. He drew off his right glove — and Tobin saw, for a moment, the old pale scar across the palm, like a crease in paper — and then, as if he had thought better of it, drew it on again. Over the glove he wore a gauntlet of grey steel, jointed like the shell of a crab. He held it out, palm up. “Give it to me, then,” he said. “It has to be given. You know that. I’m sure you’ve written it down somewhere.” Tobin did not throw it. He did not drop it. He put it into Captain Varrick’s hand, carefully, the way you hand somebody a cup that is too full; and he let go. The flame did not go out, not the way a candle goes out, with a twist of smoke. It simply shut, like an eye closing. One moment there was a small gold bead of light in the grey gauntlet; the next there was a battered brass lamp with a cracked chimney and nothing inside it at all. No glow. No warmth. It looked like something from the bottom of a box in Silas Grubb’s pawnshop, with a ticket on it saying one lamp, damaged, a penny. All at once Tobin’s hands had stopped stinging. He had not known how much they hurt until they stopped. They felt cold now, and empty, and very far away. “There,” said Varrick softly, turning the dark lamp over. “That’s all it ever was, you see. A bit of brass. Thank you, Tobin.” “Now my father,” said Tobin. Varrick laughed. It was not a loud laugh. If it had been loud, it might have been easier. It was a small, quiet, almost friendly laugh, the kind a grown-up gives when a child says something funny without meaning to. “Freed?” he said. “Your father? Boy, your father bargained with her and lost. People who bargain with her always lose.” He tucked the lamp into the crook of his arm. “You should know that. You just did.” The words went into Tobin’s ears and lay there, like stones dropped into deep water, and for a moment nothing happened. Then they reached the bottom. “But the ring,” he said. “The letter. It was his writing—“ “Oh, all quite true,” said Varrick. “He is in a cell; he did write to you; he is sorry. I never tell a lie when the truth will do the work, Tobin. It so seldom fails.” He drew his grey cloak about him. “He promised her this lamp, and could not deliver it, and she does not forgive people who fail her. She will find it very funny, I think, that his son did what he could not.” Something in Tobin broke loose. He was not a fighting sort of boy. He had been a disappointment to his father in the fencing-room every Thursday for six years. But he threw himself at Captain Varrick now, with his burned hands out, grabbing for the lamp. It was like running into a wall. Varrick did not even seem to hurry. He moved one arm — that was all — and Tobin went flying sideways out through the open door and struck the iron rail of the gallery with his shoulder. His spectacles went skidding away, and for one sick, endless moment he saw the sea, very far down, white on the black rock, through the bars. Varrick stood over him, a tall grey blur against the white. “Don’t be tiresome,” he said. “You’ve done your part. I’m taking this down to the Great Forge, under the city. Old Venn’s people built it very finely; I don’t think he has ever been quite sure what it is for.” There was a smile in his voice. “This lamp is going to be laid on the anvil and pressed into the Queen’s greatest stone. A glowstone made from the last true Flame.” He paused, as if he could see it already. “Think how it will shine.” His footsteps went away, unhurried, round and round and down the stair, until Tobin could not hear them any more. He lay there a long time. When at last he sat up, he found his spectacles by feel, with one lens cracked across, and put them on. The room swam back: the white floor, the iron rail, the great white stone blazing overhead. His coat lay crumpled where he had dropped it, empty. His palms were red and shiny and sore, and blisters were coming up on his fingers, where he had held the lamp all the long way down the harbour wall. He had carried it all that way, burning, because he had wanted his father back so badly. And his father was not coming back. Ash was still in a cell. Wren was sitting, perhaps at this very moment, in a warm kitchen on Lantern Steps, not knowing that the drawer by her bed was empty. The pendant lay against his throat, cool and smooth and kind. It doesn’t matter so very much, it seemed to say. Nothing does, if you don’t let it. It is easier not to feel. Tobin took hold of it and pulled. The fine white chain bit into his neck, and gave way at the knot with a little snap. He got to his feet, holding the rail, and looked at the small cold stone in his hand. It shone up at him, white and perfect and quite indifferent. He threw it as hard as he could out over the rail. It went turning down through the evening, a tiny white spark, smaller and smaller, and was gone into the sea without a sound. And then it was as if the stone had been holding a door shut in him, all those days, and now there was nothing holding it. Everything came through at once. His father, writing I was wrong. Wren on the waystone with her shoulder against his, cracking Nettle’s bread like a nut. The landlady on the step: I hardly know him, really. The man with the crab-pot, and his own voice saying, loud and clear, I don’t know him. Ash, who had stepped in front of him in the dry stream-bed and taken the hurt that was meant for him, and told him afterwards that fear was not the same as cowardice. Ash, whom he did not know. Somewhere far out over the darkening water, a gull cried, once; and then again, thin and sharp and lonely. Tobin sank down on the cold floor of the lighthouse, with his burned hands over his face, and wept bitterly. I will not tell you any more about that hour. Some things belong only to the person they happen to. But I will tell you this, because it matters for what comes after: it was the kind of weeping that is not the end of a person. It only feels like it. Far below him, under the white city, in the place where the dark was pressed into stone, the great pale hammers were falling.

fields.title: Into the Glowstone Mines
fields.body_html:
The town gaol of Vaelport was the cleanest prison in Gloamhaven. It had white walls and a white floor and white bars, and a glowstone in every corridor, so that the prisoners could never once, by day or night, get away from the light. Most of them had stopped trying. They sat in their cells with their hands in their laps and looked at nothing, and gave the gaoler no trouble at all.

The prisoner in the end cell was different. He sat on his bench with his bad leg stretched out in front of him, and his long hands folded on his knee, and he hummed. He hummed it out of tune, because there was nobody to mind. Now and then he said “Hm” to the wall, as if the wall had said something foolish.

The gaoler, who was young and tired and had a cold, had been told that the old man was mad. He was beginning to think it was catching.

That evening, as the tide turned, the gaoler sat at his table at the end of the corridor with his supper in front of him — a heel of bread, a slab of cheese, and one round sugared biscuit, which he was saving — and his chair tipped back against the wall, and his great iron ring of keys hanging from his belt on a leather thong. And because it was warm in the guardroom, and he had been on duty since dawn, and the white light never changed, his chin went down, and down, until it rested on his chest.

Something small and grey came in under the door.

It came in flat, like a draught. It crossed the white floor without a sound. It stopped by the table, and sat up, and looked at the gaoler’s supper with great seriousness; and the spark at the end of its tail, which had been very small and dim for days, glowed a little brighter.

Cinder, I am afraid, had her priorities. She took the biscuit first.

She ate it in three bites under the table, and licked up the crumbs, and sneezed once, very quietly, at the glowstone in the corridor, which she disliked on principle. Then she turned her attention to the keys.

The ring hung from the gaoler’s belt by its thong, just out of reach. Cinder stood on her hind legs, and put her front paws delicately on the gaoler’s knee, and began to chew.

The gaoler snored. Cinder chewed. The gaoler stirred, and muttered, “Not now, Mother, I’ve done the step,” and Cinder froze with the thong between her teeth and her ears flat, and the gaoler sank down again; and the thong parted; and the great ring of keys slid off the belt and into Cinder’s jaws with a clank that would have woken anybody who was not very tired indeed.

She dragged it down the corridor, clink, clank, clink, though it was nearly as big as she was. In the cells along the way, grey faces turned slowly to watch her go by, and turned slowly back again.

At the end cell, Old Ash was waiting at the bars.

“Hm,” he said. “You took your time.”

Cinder pushed the keys through the bars with her nose and sat down, very pleased with herself, and sneezed a small shower of sparks onto his boots.

It took Ash some while to find the right key, because there were forty of them. When he had found it, and let himself out, and fetched his two poles from the rack in the guardroom where they had been leaning, he stopped beside the sleeping gaoler. He looked at the empty plate. He looked at Cinder, who looked back at him with no shame whatever.

He took a crust out of his own coat pocket, and laid it where the biscuit had been. Then he hung the ring of keys carefully on the back of the gaoler’s chair, so that the lad would not be blamed for losing them.

“Come along, girl,” he said. “Something’s wrong. I can feel it in my leg.” He leaned on his poles and listened, with his head up, the way Cinder listened. “Something’s gone cold that oughtn’t to be.”

Wren and Mira were on the harbour front, by the fish-market, where the gulls stood about on the bollards looking for somebody to blame.

They had been everywhere looking for Tobin: the upturned boat, the end of the fish-quay, up and down Lantern Steps twice. They had left Pim sitting by the Pellows’ fire with a blanket round her, staring at it, and Mrs Pellow kneeling beside her holding a cup of milk that Pim did not drink.

And all that time the singing-stone in Wren’s pocket had been humming.

It had begun very softly, in Tobin’s empty room. It had grown louder ever since. Now it was a low, steady, trembling note that Wren could feel through the cloth of her coat, against her leg, like a cat purring — only there was nothing friendly in it at all. It was the sound it had made on the Greywaste when the Hollow courier came. It was the sound of cold, let loose.

“I don’t understand,” Wren kept saying. “I don’t understand.”

She had said it so many times that the words had worn smooth. Mira had stopped answering. She only held on to Wren’s sleeve, and listened.

Then Mira lifted her head and said, “Oh. Wren. Two sticks, and a step, and two sticks. And something small with claws.”

Wren turned round.

Old Ash was coming along the harbour front towards them, slow on his two poles, with Cinder trotting at his heel; and the white light lay on his patched coat and his singed beard and made him look very old and very thin. Wren had not seen him since the market square. She had not known how much she wanted to until that moment. She ran at him, and very nearly knocked him over, and held on to his coat with both fists.

“Steady,” said Ash. “Steady, child. One good leg, remember.” But he let go of one pole and put his hand on her hair.

“How did you get out?”

“Cinder had a word with the gaoler.” He looked down at her. “Where’s the lamp, Wren?”

Wren let go of his coat.

She told him. She told it badly, all out of order — the drawer, and the empty handkerchief, and Mrs Pellow saying so happily that Tobin had come by to see how she was getting on, and how he’d gone up to fetch a book, and gone off without his coat. The inn. The bed. She took the compass out of her pocket and held it out to him, and her hand was shaking.

“He wouldn’t,” she said. “Would he? Not Tobin. He’s — he’s Tobin. He wouldn’t.”

Ash took the compass. He opened the lid and looked at it. The needle swung, and settled: north and a bit east. He looked at it for a long time.

And Wren, watching his face, saw something happen to it that she had never seen before.

She had expected him to be angry. She had seen Ash angry; it was like weather coming over a hill. But it was not anger. It was something much quieter, and much worse. It was the face of a man who has been told of a death. Just for a moment, all the lines in it went down at once.

“Oh, lad,” said Old Ash, very low. “Oh, my poor lad.”

Then he shut the compass, and gave it back to her, and his face was his own again — stern and tired and sure.

“Varrick,” he said. “It’ll have been Varrick. He’ll have offered the boy his father.” He drew a long breath. “Hm. And he’ll not drown it, or break it. That’s not her way. She’ll want it made into one of hers.” He looked past them, along the harbour front, to where the long white sheds of the Glowstone Company stood by the water, with their chimneys that gave no smoke. “Down there. Under the city. The Forge.”

“Then we’ll go and get it,” said Wren.

“I’ll go and get it,” said Ash. “You’ll stay here.”

“Rot!”

“You’ll stay here,” said Ash, “with Mira, and you’ll look for Tobin. Somebody must. He’ll need finding tonight more than any of us.” He looked at her, and his eyes under their white brows were very steady. “Don’t hate him yet, child. You’ll want all your strength for other things.”

And before Wren could think of an answer, he had turned on his two poles and was going away along the white quay, slow and lame, towards the sheds; and Cinder went with him.

Wren stood and watched him go.

“Well?” said Mira, after a moment.

“Well what?”

“Well, are we staying here, as we were told?” said Mira. “Or are we following him at a sensible distance, as you were going to suggest?”

Wren looked at her. Then she took the singing-stone out of her pocket. It was humming so hard now that it buzzed in her palm like a trapped bee.

“I wasn’t going to suggest anything,” she said. “Come on.”

They went in at shift-change, the way Tobin and Ash had gone in before them days ago, through a side-gate in the yard of the Company’s works, among the long silent line of miners going down.

Nobody stopped them. Nobody so much as looked at them. The miners walked in a slow grey file, men and women both, with their tools on their shoulders and their eyes on the back of the person in front, and they did not speak, and they did not hurry. Wren had seen people like that before: sitting on doorsteps in Soot Lane, the night the Ring failed, with the colour gone out of them. But these people were walking. These people had jobs. That was somehow the most horrible thing of all.

The tunnel went down. And the further down it went, the brighter it grew.

At first there were glowstones set in the walls here and there, like lamps along a street. Then there were more of them. Then the walls were glowstone — raw, uncut, great white veins of it running through the rock — and the light came at Wren from every side at once, from above and below and behind, so that there were no shadows anywhere and no edges to anything. The floor was white and the walls were white and the roof was white, and they all ran together, so that she could not tell where one stopped and the next began.

Her eyes began to water. She screwed them up. It made no difference. She put her hand up to shade them, and the light came round the sides of it.

Then she walked into a wall.

She did not see it coming. One moment there was white in front of her, and the next there was white against her nose, very hard, and she sat down.

“Blast,” said Wren, holding her nose.

“There is a wall there,” said Mira helpfully.

“I know there’s a wall there, I’ve just met it.” Wren got up, and blinked, and tried to look round. It was no good. Everything was white. It was worse than the dark, where at least you know that you cannot see. Her eyes kept telling her that she could see, and then showing her nothing. Somewhere ahead she could hear Ash’s poles, tock, tock, going away from them, and the shuffling feet of the miners, and the stone humming in her pocket. She could not tell which way any of it was.

“Mira,” she said, and her voice came out small. “I can’t. I can’t see anything. It’s too bright. I can’t see a thing.”

“No,” said Mira. “I don’t suppose you can.”

She had stopped beside Wren. And Wren, squinting at her through her streaming eyes, saw that Mira was standing quite easily, with her head up and her face calm, and that her eyes were shut.

“Give me your hand,” said Mira.

“What are you doing? You’ll walk us both into—“

“I don’t need it to be dark, Wren,” said Mira. “I only need to not look.”

She clicked her tongue — tk-tk — and listened, and turned her head a little to the left, and clicked again. And Wren remembered, all in a rush, the Deeps: the Whispering Galleries, black as the inside of a boot, and Mira walking ahead of them all with her eyes open on nothing, finding the way by echoes. Mira had lived her whole life in the dark. She had only had her eyes for a few weeks. She had not forgotten how to do without them.

Wren held out her hand. Mira took it.

“Now shut yours,” said Mira. “It will be easier. You won’t keep trying to believe them.”

Wren shut her eyes. The white went red and then dim behind her lids, and it was such a relief that she nearly cried.

They went on.

It was the strangest walk of Wren’s life, and she had walked through some strange places. Mira went first, clicking softly, and Wren came behind with her eyes shut, holding Mira’s hand, the way Tobin had held Mira’s sleeve in the dark on the way to Deepholm. Every now and then Mira said, “Step down,” or “Duck,” or “There’s a miner coming; stand still,” and Wren did as she was told. Once a grey shoulder brushed past her, cold as a gravestone, and went on without a pause. Once the tunnel forked, and Mira stood clicking for a long moment, and then said, “Left. That way is longer, and it goes down. And the poles went this way.”

“You can hear that?”

“I can hear his poles,” said Mira, “and I can hear your stone. They’re going the same way.”

The singing-stone was humming louder now. It hummed so loud that Wren’s whole pocket shook with it. And the air was changing. It had been cold before, the flat dead cold of Vaelport’s light; but now there was another cold coming up from below to meet them, and Wren knew that one. She had met it in Soot Lane, and on the Greywaste, and in the Galleries of the Deeps. It was a cold that was not just the absence of warmth. It was a cold that wanted something.

Cinder came trotting back to them out of the white, sneezing furiously at every glowstone she passed, and pushed her nose into Wren’s hand, and trotted on again.

“She says hurry,” said Mira.

“She does not.”

“She does. Listen to her feet.”

They hurried.

“If you walk me into a wall,” said Wren, through her teeth, stumbling, “I’ll never speak to you again.”

“You walked yourself into three before I started,” said Mira. “I think I am allowed one.”

And despite everything — despite the drawer, and the empty handkerchief, and Tobin’s bed not slept in, and the cold coming up from below — Wren very nearly laughed. It stuck in her chest and never quite got out. But I tell you this because it is worth knowing: even in the worst places, a friend can make you very nearly laugh. It is not nothing. Sometimes it is a great deal.

The tunnel ended quite suddenly.

Mira stopped. Wren bumped into her. Mira clicked once, and then again, and then she let out a long, slow breath, and held Wren’s hand very tight.

“It’s very big,” she whispered. “It’s the biggest place I’ve ever heard. Bigger than the Great Echo-Hall. And there’s a — a sound in the middle. Going up. Like wind in a chimney, only cold. Wren, you can open your eyes. It’s not so bright here. Not in the middle.”

Wren opened her eyes.

They were standing on a narrow iron gallery, high up on the wall of an enormous round chamber. The walls all round were glowstone, white and blazing, as bright as the tunnels had been. But the middle of the chamber was not bright. The middle of the chamber was the darkest thing Wren had ever seen.

It was a shaft. A great round black shaft in the floor, as wide as a mill-pond; and up out of it, slowly, endlessly, came the dark. It came up like smoke from a chimney, thick and cold and grey-black, rolling and folding over on itself, and the cold of it reached Wren even up on the gallery, so that her breath smoked and her fingers went numb on the rail. It made no sound of its own. But all round the rim of the shaft stood the hammers.

They were huge — pale as bone, each as big as a cart, hung on great chains from the roof — and they rose and fell, slow and steady as a heartbeat, on the dark that rolled onto the anvils round the rim. Each time they rose, something small and white and shining lay where the dark had been, and a grey figure stepped forward and carried it away.

“That’s it,” Wren whispered. “What Tobin saw.”

The singing-stone in her pocket was not humming any more. It was keening, high and thin, like a kettle.

Out on the forge floor, between the black shaft and the gallery, stood one anvil bigger than all the rest, with one hammer hanging over it bigger than all the rest; and beside it stood a tall man in grey armour and a grey cloak.

Wren could not see his face from so high. She did not need to. She knew the set of his shoulders. She had seen it on the top of the Great Beacon in Emberwick, and at the edge of the market square, half in shadow, rubbing his palm.

Captain Varrick held something small in his grey gauntlet. He looked at it a moment. Then he set it down on the great anvil, carefully, almost gently, the way you set down a cup.

It was a little battered brass lamp with a cracked chimney. And it was dark.

Wren made a sound. She did not know she had made it. Mira’s hand closed on hers like a trap.

High over the anvil, the great pale hammer had stopped at the top of its swing, and hung there, waiting.

And then, from the far side of the forge floor, out of the mouth of a low tunnel, came a sound that Wren would have known anywhere in the world.

Tock. A step. Tock.

Old Ash came out into the light. He was alone. He was very lame. He leaned on his two poles, and set them down, and swung himself forward on them, and set them down again; and he came out across the wide white floor of the Great Forge, between the falling hammers, towards the tall grey man at the anvil, slowly, without stopping, the way he had walked the wall at Emberwick every night for thirty years to light the lamps that nobody else would light.

Varrick turned round and saw him coming.

And Old Ash, very tall and very thin and very old, lifted his head and spoke one word across the forge; and it carried, the way the Galleries had carried words in the Deeps, all the way up to the gallery where the two girls stood.

“Lad,” he said.
fields.body_text: The town gaol of Vaelport was the cleanest prison in Gloamhaven. It had white walls and a white floor and white bars, and a glowstone in every corridor, so that the prisoners could never once, by day or night, get away from the light. Most of them had stopped trying. They sat in their cells with their hands in their laps and looked at nothing, and gave the gaoler no trouble at all. The prisoner in the end cell was different. He sat on his bench with his bad leg stretched out in front of him, and his long hands folded on his knee, and he hummed. He hummed it out of tune, because there was nobody to mind. Now and then he said “Hm” to the wall, as if the wall had said something foolish. The gaoler, who was young and tired and had a cold, had been told that the old man was mad. He was beginning to think it was catching. That evening, as the tide turned, the gaoler sat at his table at the end of the corridor with his supper in front of him — a heel of bread, a slab of cheese, and one round sugared biscuit, which he was saving — and his chair tipped back against the wall, and his great iron ring of keys hanging from his belt on a leather thong. And because it was warm in the guardroom, and he had been on duty since dawn, and the white light never changed, his chin went down, and down, until it rested on his chest. Something small and grey came in under the door. It came in flat, like a draught. It crossed the white floor without a sound. It stopped by the table, and sat up, and looked at the gaoler’s supper with great seriousness; and the spark at the end of its tail, which had been very small and dim for days, glowed a little brighter. Cinder, I am afraid, had her priorities. She took the biscuit first. She ate it in three bites under the table, and licked up the crumbs, and sneezed once, very quietly, at the glowstone in the corridor, which she disliked on principle. Then she turned her attention to the keys. The ring hung from the gaoler’s belt by its thong, just out of reach. Cinder stood on her hind legs, and put her front paws delicately on the gaoler’s knee, and began to chew. The gaoler snored. Cinder chewed. The gaoler stirred, and muttered, “Not now, Mother, I’ve done the step,” and Cinder froze with the thong between her teeth and her ears flat, and the gaoler sank down again; and the thong parted; and the great ring of keys slid off the belt and into Cinder’s jaws with a clank that would have woken anybody who was not very tired indeed. She dragged it down the corridor, clink, clank, clink, though it was nearly as big as she was. In the cells along the way, grey faces turned slowly to watch her go by, and turned slowly back again. At the end cell, Old Ash was waiting at the bars. “Hm,” he said. “You took your time.” Cinder pushed the keys through the bars with her nose and sat down, very pleased with herself, and sneezed a small shower of sparks onto his boots. It took Ash some while to find the right key, because there were forty of them. When he had found it, and let himself out, and fetched his two poles from the rack in the guardroom where they had been leaning, he stopped beside the sleeping gaoler. He looked at the empty plate. He looked at Cinder, who looked back at him with no shame whatever. He took a crust out of his own coat pocket, and laid it where the biscuit had been. Then he hung the ring of keys carefully on the back of the gaoler’s chair, so that the lad would not be blamed for losing them. “Come along, girl,” he said. “Something’s wrong. I can feel it in my leg.” He leaned on his poles and listened, with his head up, the way Cinder listened. “Something’s gone cold that oughtn’t to be.” Wren and Mira were on the harbour front, by the fish-market, where the gulls stood about on the bollards looking for somebody to blame. They had been everywhere looking for Tobin: the upturned boat, the end of the fish-quay, up and down Lantern Steps twice. They had left Pim sitting by the Pellows’ fire with a blanket round her, staring at it, and Mrs Pellow kneeling beside her holding a cup of milk that Pim did not drink. And all that time the singing-stone in Wren’s pocket had been humming. It had begun very softly, in Tobin’s empty room. It had grown louder ever since. Now it was a low, steady, trembling note that Wren could feel through the cloth of her coat, against her leg, like a cat purring — only there was nothing friendly in it at all. It was the sound it had made on the Greywaste when the Hollow courier came. It was the sound of cold, let loose. “I don’t understand,” Wren kept saying. “I don’t understand.” She had said it so many times that the words had worn smooth. Mira had stopped answering. She only held on to Wren’s sleeve, and listened. Then Mira lifted her head and said, “Oh. Wren. Two sticks, and a step, and two sticks. And something small with claws.” Wren turned round. Old Ash was coming along the harbour front towards them, slow on his two poles, with Cinder trotting at his heel; and the white light lay on his patched coat and his singed beard and made him look very old and very thin. Wren had not seen him since the market square. She had not known how much she wanted to until that moment. She ran at him, and very nearly knocked him over, and held on to his coat with both fists. “Steady,” said Ash. “Steady, child. One good leg, remember.” But he let go of one pole and put his hand on her hair. “How did you get out?” “Cinder had a word with the gaoler.” He looked down at her. “Where’s the lamp, Wren?” Wren let go of his coat. She told him. She told it badly, all out of order — the drawer, and the empty handkerchief, and Mrs Pellow saying so happily that Tobin had come by to see how she was getting on, and how he’d gone up to fetch a book, and gone off without his coat. The inn. The bed. She took the compass out of her pocket and held it out to him, and her hand was shaking. “He wouldn’t,” she said. “Would he? Not Tobin. He’s — he’s Tobin. He wouldn’t.” Ash took the compass. He opened the lid and looked at it. The needle swung, and settled: north and a bit east. He looked at it for a long time. And Wren, watching his face, saw something happen to it that she had never seen before. She had expected him to be angry. She had seen Ash angry; it was like weather coming over a hill. But it was not anger. It was something much quieter, and much worse. It was the face of a man who has been told of a death. Just for a moment, all the lines in it went down at once. “Oh, lad,” said Old Ash, very low. “Oh, my poor lad.” Then he shut the compass, and gave it back to her, and his face was his own again — stern and tired and sure. “Varrick,” he said. “It’ll have been Varrick. He’ll have offered the boy his father.” He drew a long breath. “Hm. And he’ll not drown it, or break it. That’s not her way. She’ll want it made into one of hers.” He looked past them, along the harbour front, to where the long white sheds of the Glowstone Company stood by the water, with their chimneys that gave no smoke. “Down there. Under the city. The Forge.” “Then we’ll go and get it,” said Wren. “I’ll go and get it,” said Ash. “You’ll stay here.” “Rot!” “You’ll stay here,” said Ash, “with Mira, and you’ll look for Tobin. Somebody must. He’ll need finding tonight more than any of us.” He looked at her, and his eyes under their white brows were very steady. “Don’t hate him yet, child. You’ll want all your strength for other things.” And before Wren could think of an answer, he had turned on his two poles and was going away along the white quay, slow and lame, towards the sheds; and Cinder went with him. Wren stood and watched him go. “Well?” said Mira, after a moment. “Well what?” “Well, are we staying here, as we were told?” said Mira. “Or are we following him at a sensible distance, as you were going to suggest?” Wren looked at her. Then she took the singing-stone out of her pocket. It was humming so hard now that it buzzed in her palm like a trapped bee. “I wasn’t going to suggest anything,” she said. “Come on.” They went in at shift-change, the way Tobin and Ash had gone in before them days ago, through a side-gate in the yard of the Company’s works, among the long silent line of miners going down. Nobody stopped them. Nobody so much as looked at them. The miners walked in a slow grey file, men and women both, with their tools on their shoulders and their eyes on the back of the person in front, and they did not speak, and they did not hurry. Wren had seen people like that before: sitting on doorsteps in Soot Lane, the night the Ring failed, with the colour gone out of them. But these people were walking. These people had jobs. That was somehow the most horrible thing of all. The tunnel went down. And the further down it went, the brighter it grew. At first there were glowstones set in the walls here and there, like lamps along a street. Then there were more of them. Then the walls were glowstone — raw, uncut, great white veins of it running through the rock — and the light came at Wren from every side at once, from above and below and behind, so that there were no shadows anywhere and no edges to anything. The floor was white and the walls were white and the roof was white, and they all ran together, so that she could not tell where one stopped and the next began. Her eyes began to water. She screwed them up. It made no difference. She put her hand up to shade them, and the light came round the sides of it. Then she walked into a wall. She did not see it coming. One moment there was white in front of her, and the next there was white against her nose, very hard, and she sat down. “Blast,” said Wren, holding her nose. “There is a wall there,” said Mira helpfully. “I know there’s a wall there, I’ve just met it.” Wren got up, and blinked, and tried to look round. It was no good. Everything was white. It was worse than the dark, where at least you know that you cannot see. Her eyes kept telling her that she could see, and then showing her nothing. Somewhere ahead she could hear Ash’s poles, tock, tock, going away from them, and the shuffling feet of the miners, and the stone humming in her pocket. She could not tell which way any of it was. “Mira,” she said, and her voice came out small. “I can’t. I can’t see anything. It’s too bright. I can’t see a thing.” “No,” said Mira. “I don’t suppose you can.” She had stopped beside Wren. And Wren, squinting at her through her streaming eyes, saw that Mira was standing quite easily, with her head up and her face calm, and that her eyes were shut. “Give me your hand,” said Mira. “What are you doing? You’ll walk us both into—“ “I don’t need it to be dark, Wren,” said Mira. “I only need to not look.” She clicked her tongue — tk-tk — and listened, and turned her head a little to the left, and clicked again. And Wren remembered, all in a rush, the Deeps: the Whispering Galleries, black as the inside of a boot, and Mira walking ahead of them all with her eyes open on nothing, finding the way by echoes. Mira had lived her whole life in the dark. She had only had her eyes for a few weeks. She had not forgotten how to do without them. Wren held out her hand. Mira took it. “Now shut yours,” said Mira. “It will be easier. You won’t keep trying to believe them.” Wren shut her eyes. The white went red and then dim behind her lids, and it was such a relief that she nearly cried. They went on. It was the strangest walk of Wren’s life, and she had walked through some strange places. Mira went first, clicking softly, and Wren came behind with her eyes shut, holding Mira’s hand, the way Tobin had held Mira’s sleeve in the dark on the way to Deepholm. Every now and then Mira said, “Step down,” or “Duck,” or “There’s a miner coming; stand still,” and Wren did as she was told. Once a grey shoulder brushed past her, cold as a gravestone, and went on without a pause. Once the tunnel forked, and Mira stood clicking for a long moment, and then said, “Left. That way is longer, and it goes down. And the poles went this way.” “You can hear that?” “I can hear his poles,” said Mira, “and I can hear your stone. They’re going the same way.” The singing-stone was humming louder now. It hummed so loud that Wren’s whole pocket shook with it. And the air was changing. It had been cold before, the flat dead cold of Vaelport’s light; but now there was another cold coming up from below to meet them, and Wren knew that one. She had met it in Soot Lane, and on the Greywaste, and in the Galleries of the Deeps. It was a cold that was not just the absence of warmth. It was a cold that wanted something. Cinder came trotting back to them out of the white, sneezing furiously at every glowstone she passed, and pushed her nose into Wren’s hand, and trotted on again. “She says hurry,” said Mira. “She does not.” “She does. Listen to her feet.” They hurried. “If you walk me into a wall,” said Wren, through her teeth, stumbling, “I’ll never speak to you again.” “You walked yourself into three before I started,” said Mira. “I think I am allowed one.” And despite everything — despite the drawer, and the empty handkerchief, and Tobin’s bed not slept in, and the cold coming up from below — Wren very nearly laughed. It stuck in her chest and never quite got out. But I tell you this because it is worth knowing: even in the worst places, a friend can make you very nearly laugh. It is not nothing. Sometimes it is a great deal. The tunnel ended quite suddenly. Mira stopped. Wren bumped into her. Mira clicked once, and then again, and then she let out a long, slow breath, and held Wren’s hand very tight. “It’s very big,” she whispered. “It’s the biggest place I’ve ever heard. Bigger than the Great Echo-Hall. And there’s a — a sound in the middle. Going up. Like wind in a chimney, only cold. Wren, you can open your eyes. It’s not so bright here. Not in the middle.” Wren opened her eyes. They were standing on a narrow iron gallery, high up on the wall of an enormous round chamber. The walls all round were glowstone, white and blazing, as bright as the tunnels had been. But the middle of the chamber was not bright. The middle of the chamber was the darkest thing Wren had ever seen. It was a shaft. A great round black shaft in the floor, as wide as a mill-pond; and up out of it, slowly, endlessly, came the dark. It came up like smoke from a chimney, thick and cold and grey-black, rolling and folding over on itself, and the cold of it reached Wren even up on the gallery, so that her breath smoked and her fingers went numb on the rail. It made no sound of its own. But all round the rim of the shaft stood the hammers. They were huge — pale as bone, each as big as a cart, hung on great chains from the roof — and they rose and fell, slow and steady as a heartbeat, on the dark that rolled onto the anvils round the rim. Each time they rose, something small and white and shining lay where the dark had been, and a grey figure stepped forward and carried it away. “That’s it,” Wren whispered. “What Tobin saw.” The singing-stone in her pocket was not humming any more. It was keening, high and thin, like a kettle. Out on the forge floor, between the black shaft and the gallery, stood one anvil bigger than all the rest, with one hammer hanging over it bigger than all the rest; and beside it stood a tall man in grey armour and a grey cloak. Wren could not see his face from so high. She did not need to. She knew the set of his shoulders. She had seen it on the top of the Great Beacon in Emberwick, and at the edge of the market square, half in shadow, rubbing his palm. Captain Varrick held something small in his grey gauntlet. He looked at it a moment. Then he set it down on the great anvil, carefully, almost gently, the way you set down a cup. It was a little battered brass lamp with a cracked chimney. And it was dark. Wren made a sound. She did not know she had made it. Mira’s hand closed on hers like a trap. High over the anvil, the great pale hammer had stopped at the top of its swing, and hung there, waiting. And then, from the far side of the forge floor, out of the mouth of a low tunnel, came a sound that Wren would have known anywhere in the world. Tock. A step. Tock. Old Ash came out into the light. He was alone. He was very lame. He leaned on his two poles, and set them down, and swung himself forward on them, and set them down again; and he came out across the wide white floor of the Great Forge, between the falling hammers, towards the tall grey man at the anvil, slowly, without stopping, the way he had walked the wall at Emberwick every night for thirty years to light the lamps that nobody else would light. Varrick turned round and saw him coming. And Old Ash, very tall and very thin and very old, lifted his head and spoke one word across the forge; and it carried, the way the Galleries had carried words in the Deeps, all the way up to the gallery where the two girls stood. “Lad,” he said.

fields.title: Old Ash’s Last Lamp
fields.body_html:
This is the part of the story that Wren never liked to tell.

She told it in the end, of course, many years afterwards, to people who needed to hear it. But she always told it quickly, and plainly, looking at her hands; and when she had finished she would get up and go and see to the fire, whether it needed seeing to or not. So I shall tell it the way she did, as plainly as I can. You may see to the fire afterwards, if you like.

The great hammer hung over the anvil, and did not fall.

All round the black shaft the other hammers went on rising and falling, slow and steady, and the dark went on rolling up out of the shaft, and the grey smiths went on carrying the new white stones away. Nobody looked up. Nobody but Varrick turned to see the lame old man coming across the floor. And Ash came on, tock, step, tock, until he stood on the other side of the great anvil, and leaned on his poles, and got his breath.

“Old man,” said Varrick. His voice was as smooth as ever. “You ought to be in a cell.”

“Hm. I was,” said Ash. “The company was poor. I left.”

He looked down at the little brass lamp lying dark on the anvil between them. Then he looked up again at the tall grey man, and Wren, up on the gallery, saw his face; and there was nothing in it that she had expected. No anger. No fear. Only a great tiredness, and under the tiredness, something very like love.

“You’ve grown thin, lad,” said Old Ash. “Does nobody feed you, in her service?”

“I want for nothing.”

“No,” said Ash. “I don’t suppose you do. That’s always been the trouble with her bargains. You never want for anything again. You only stop wanting.” He shifted on his poles. “Do you still take three sugars in your tea?”

Something flickered at the corner of Varrick’s mouth, and was gone. “Not in yours. I never did. Nobody could.”

“Hm,” said Ash, and almost smiled. “That’s fair.”

Then he let go of one of his poles — it leaned against the anvil — and held out his empty hand, palm up, across the lamp.

“Show me your hand, lad.”

Varrick did not move.

“You know which one,” said Ash gently. “The right. Take off that glove and show me.”

For a long moment nothing happened. The hammers rose and fell. The dark rolled up out of the shaft. And then, slowly, as if somebody else were doing it, Captain Varrick drew the grey gauntlet off his right hand, and the glove beneath it, and turned his hand over.

The scar lay across the palm, old and white and puckered, from one side to the other.

“I put that there,” said Ash. “Do you remember? I held the oath-flame, and you put your hand over it, and you said the words — freely given, freely given. You didn’t flinch. You were sixteen, and so proud you could hardly stand still.” His voice was very quiet, but the great round chamber carried it, every word. “And the next night I took you up on the wall at Emberwick, and gave you the taper, and let you light your first Ring-lamp on your own. Do you remember that? Your hands were shaking so, I thought you’d drop it over the parapet. And the wick caught, and the lamp went up gold all at once, and you laughed. Out loud. On the wall, at midnight. Half the Watch came running to see what was the matter.” He paused. “I’ve never heard a better sound in my life. Not before or since.”

Varrick was looking at his own palm.

“That boy,” said Ash, “is not dead. I’ve told you before. I never buried him. Pick up the lamp, lad. Not for her. Give it back to the girl, and come home. It isn’t too late. It’s never too late, while you can still hear me.”

Wren held her breath. Up on the gallery, Mira’s fingers were crushing hers; Cinder was pressed against her legs, trembling.

And Varrick hesitated.

It was not a heartbeat this time. It was longer than that — much longer — so long that Wren began to believe, really to believe, that something was going to happen. His left hand had come up and closed over his scarred right palm, and was holding it, hard, the way you hold a burn. His head had bent. He stood there by the anvil, in the cold white light, and for the length of a long slow breath he looked like what he must once have been: a young man on a wall, at midnight, with a taper in his hand.

Ash did not say anything more. He only waited, leaning on his one pole, as if he had all the time in the world, and meant to spend every bit of it here.

Then his face closed.

It closed the way a door closes in a big house, far away down a corridor: quietly, without a slam, but quite finally. He let go of his palm. He did not put the glove back on.

“You talk too much, old man,” he said. “You always did.”

And he struck.

He did it fast, the way a snake does it. His bare hand swept the leaning pole away from the anvil, and the other pole out from under Ash’s arm, and the old man, who had only one good leg and nothing now to stand on, went down. He fell hard against the great anvil, and slid, and caught at the edge of it to save himself.

Wren screamed. She did not know she was going to. She was already running — along the gallery, to where an iron stair went down the wall, and down it, three steps at a time, with Mira behind her clicking and Cinder ahead of them both, a grey streak with a spark for a tail.

And Old Ash, on his knees at the anvil, reached up over the edge of it with one long hand, and his fingers closed on the lamp.

He did not hold it to his chest. He did not hold it up against Varrick, or the hammers, or the dark. He turned on his knees, and he looked for Wren, and he found her — a small dark shape pelting down the iron stair — and he held the lamp out towards her, at the full length of his arm, the way he had once held out a cup of dreadful tea to a frightened chimney-sweep at his table, without asking anything at all.

“Wren,” he said. “Here, child. Here. Take it.”

And the lamp blazed.

I do not know how to tell you how bright it was. Nobody who was there could ever tell it properly either.

It was not like the white light of the glowstones. It did not glare, or dazzle, or make your eyes water. It was gold — deep, warm, living gold — and it filled the Great Forge from wall to wall in one breath, the way the sun fills a room when somebody throws back the curtains. And where it went, colour came back. The white floor was suddenly warm grey stone with veins of rust-red in it. The chains of the hammers were black iron with brown in the links. Mira’s dress was blue. Cinder’s coat was the grey of old ashes, warm and soft, and her tail-spark flared up like a struck match. And Old Ash’s coat, his old patched coat, which even by the lamp had only ever been a tired blue-grey — Ash’s coat was blue. A deep, clear, glad blue, like the sky must have been once, before the curse: Lamplighter blue, as it had been on the day it was new. Wren had not known it could be.

The great hammer over the anvil shuddered on its chain, and stopped.

Then all the hammers stopped, all round the shaft, one after another, high in the air, and hung there.

And the shaft screamed.

You will remember, if you have read the earlier parts of this story, that the Hollows make no sound, except one. Wren had heard it in Soot Lane, and on the Beacon, and in the Deeps. It came now out of the black shaft, out of the rolling dark itself, a long thin shriek that went on and on and set every tooth in her head aching. The dark in the shaft heaved and boiled and drew back from the gold like a hand from a stove.

And all round the walls of the Great Forge, the glowstones began to crack.

They cracked the way ice cracks on a pond in spring — with a sharp, singing crack here, and another there, and then a great many all at once, running across the walls in white lines. And out of every crack came a thread of grey-black cold, curling, loose, like smoke from a snuffed wick. The singing-stone in Wren’s pocket went from a keen to a shriek of its own. The white light of the walls flickered — and dimmed — and went out in patches, so that for the first time since they had come to Vaelport there were shadows, long and black and jumping. And the whole chamber shook.

The grey smiths round the shaft had stopped too. They stood with their tongs hanging from their hands, and in the gold light Wren saw their faces change — not much; only a little; the way a sleeper’s face changes when somebody says his name. One of them, a big woman with a scarf over her hair, put up her hand and touched her own cheek, as though she had felt something there that she had forgotten about.

“Up!” Old Ash’s voice rang across the forge, the way it must once have rung along the wall at Emberwick on a bad night. “Up, all of you! Out! Go up to the air!”

And they went. They dropped their tongs and turned, slowly at first and then faster, stumbling, holding on to one another, and went streaming away into the tunnels towards the surface, a long grey line of them; and here and there among the grey, in the last of the gold, was a face that was not quite so grey as it had been.

Varrick had flung up his bare arm across his eyes. He stood in the gold blaze with his face turned away from it, and he cried out, once, as if the light hurt him. Perhaps it did. For one moment, through the dazzle, Wren saw him look at the old man kneeling by the anvil with the lamp held out — just one look, and she never forgot it.

Then he turned and ran. He ran into the mouth of a tunnel on the far side of the forge, where the glowstones had already gone dark, and the dark took him, and he was gone.

Wren reached Ash.

She did not remember crossing the floor. She only remembered falling on her knees beside him, and his arm coming round her, and the lamp warm and gold between them. Mira was there, clicking frantically, and Cinder was licking Ash’s face.

“Hm,” said Ash. He was breathing hard, but his eyes were bright. “I thought I told you to stay on the quay.”

“You did,” said Wren. “We didn’t.”

A stone fell from the roof, somewhere behind them, as big as a cart, and burst on the floor like a dropped jar.

“Up,” said Ash. “Up, child. My poles.”

They got him to his feet between them. Wren found one pole and Mira found the other, and they put them in his hands. Ash hung the lamp on the brass hook at the end of the right-hand pole, the way he had carried lamps along the wall at Emberwick all his life, and lifted it high, and swung himself forward; and they went across the forge floor as fast as he could go, which was not very fast at all.

Behind them the black shaft was pouring out its dark. It came up over the rim in a great slow wave and spread across the floor after them like a tide coming in over mud-flats, cold and grey and silent. Wherever it touched the gold of the lamp it shrank back; but there was so much of it, and it kept coming. The roof was falling now in earnest — not all at once, but in pieces, here and there, so that the whole chamber was full of the noise of it and of dust.

Wren could not see for the dust. Nobody could. “Shut your eyes,” said Mira, “and hold his coat,” and shut her own, and clicked, and led them — round a fallen hammer-chain lying across the floor like a dead snake, past a split anvil, between two stones that came down in the time it took to say so. Ash went between the girls, swinging on his poles, with the lamp swaying gold on its hook above their heads. He did not hurry, because he could not. He breathed like a bellows with a hole in it.

“I’ve walked the wall,” he said, between breaths, “in worse weather than this.”

“You have not,” said Wren.

“Hm,” said Ash. “No. Perhaps not.”

“The door,” said Mira. “There’s a door ahead. I can hear the draught under it. Iron. And glass.”

It stood in the wall at the top of three low steps: a great forge-door of iron bars with thick glass set between them, and beyond it a tunnel going steeply up. Ash had come in that way. It was the way out.

They went through it. Mira first, then Wren, then Cinder; and Ash last of all, slow, on his poles.

He turned in the doorway, and looked back once at the Great Forge, at the dark rolling towards him across the floor. He lifted the lamp off its hook. Then he let his poles fall, and took hold of the great door with his free hand, and swung it shut behind him; and leaned his back against it.

The dark struck the other side.

Wren felt it through the stone floor. The door jumped in its frame. Frost came racing across the glass in white feathers, and the iron bars groaned. Ash set his feet — his good one and his bad one — and leaned back, and held it.

“Ash,” said Wren. “Ash, come on—“

“Go with them, girl,” said Ash, to Cinder. Cinder was pressed against his legs, and would not move. “Go on.” And at something in his voice, she went — three steps up the tunnel, and turned, and stood there shivering, with her tail-spark gone small.

“Off you go, then,” said Ash, to the two girls. “Mind the step.”

“No,” said Wren. “No. Not without you. We’ll carry you. Mira — help me — we can carry him, he’s all bones, we can—“

The door jumped again. A crack ran across the glass behind his head.

Old Ash held out the lamp to her. Wren would not take it; she put her hands behind her back, as if that could make him come. So he reached out and took her hands, gently, and put the lamp into them, and folded her fingers round it, and held them there a moment with his own, which were very warm. He looked at her. His face, in the gold light, was not frightened at all.

“It was never mine,” he said. “It’s never been anyone’s. Give it.”

Then he let go of her hands, and set his back square against the forge-door, and lifted his head.

Mira took hold of Wren’s arm and pulled.

Wren did not remember running. She remembered the tunnel going up, steep and rough, and Mira’s hand on her arm like iron, and Cinder ahead, and the lamp blazing in her own two fists so that the walls jumped gold. She remembered looking back, once.

He was standing with his back to the door. The lamp was gone from him, and the light was going with it, up the tunnel; so that what she saw last was only an old man in a blue coat, very tall, at the bottom of a dark slope, with his head up. And for a moment — only a moment, and she never knew afterwards how she knew it — she was sure that he was not alone down there. As if someone had come to stand beside him.

“ASH!” screamed Wren.

The roof of the tunnel came down between them.

There was a long roar, and then a rumble, and then a rattle of small stones, going on and on and getting smaller. The dust came up the tunnel in a great soft rush and covered them, and they could not see, and could not breathe, and crouched against the wall with their arms over their heads.

Then the stones stopped.

There was dust, settling. That was all. Where the bottom of the tunnel had been, there was a wall of fallen rock, from floor to roof, and no way through it, and no sound behind it.

No sound at all.

Wren knelt on the stones in the dust with the lamp in her hands, and stared at the fallen rock, and did not move, and did not speak, and did not cry. She could not have told you what she was waiting for. Mira knelt beside her, with her eyes wide open and tears making two clean lines down the dust on her face, and her hand still holding on to Wren’s sleeve.

Cinder went down the slope, slowly, to the place where the rocks were. She sniffed along the bottom of them, all the way from one wall to the other, and back again. Then she sat down in front of them, very straight, with her small grey face turned up.

And she howled — once — a long, high, broken sound that went up and up the dark tunnel, and away through all the cracked and darkening mines of Vaelport, and did not come back.
fields.body_text: This is the part of the story that Wren never liked to tell. She told it in the end, of course, many years afterwards, to people who needed to hear it. But she always told it quickly, and plainly, looking at her hands; and when she had finished she would get up and go and see to the fire, whether it needed seeing to or not. So I shall tell it the way she did, as plainly as I can. You may see to the fire afterwards, if you like. The great hammer hung over the anvil, and did not fall. All round the black shaft the other hammers went on rising and falling, slow and steady, and the dark went on rolling up out of the shaft, and the grey smiths went on carrying the new white stones away. Nobody looked up. Nobody but Varrick turned to see the lame old man coming across the floor. And Ash came on, tock, step, tock, until he stood on the other side of the great anvil, and leaned on his poles, and got his breath. “Old man,” said Varrick. His voice was as smooth as ever. “You ought to be in a cell.” “Hm. I was,” said Ash. “The company was poor. I left.” He looked down at the little brass lamp lying dark on the anvil between them. Then he looked up again at the tall grey man, and Wren, up on the gallery, saw his face; and there was nothing in it that she had expected. No anger. No fear. Only a great tiredness, and under the tiredness, something very like love. “You’ve grown thin, lad,” said Old Ash. “Does nobody feed you, in her service?” “I want for nothing.” “No,” said Ash. “I don’t suppose you do. That’s always been the trouble with her bargains. You never want for anything again. You only stop wanting.” He shifted on his poles. “Do you still take three sugars in your tea?” Something flickered at the corner of Varrick’s mouth, and was gone. “Not in yours. I never did. Nobody could.” “Hm,” said Ash, and almost smiled. “That’s fair.” Then he let go of one of his poles — it leaned against the anvil — and held out his empty hand, palm up, across the lamp. “Show me your hand, lad.” Varrick did not move. “You know which one,” said Ash gently. “The right. Take off that glove and show me.” For a long moment nothing happened. The hammers rose and fell. The dark rolled up out of the shaft. And then, slowly, as if somebody else were doing it, Captain Varrick drew the grey gauntlet off his right hand, and the glove beneath it, and turned his hand over. The scar lay across the palm, old and white and puckered, from one side to the other. “I put that there,” said Ash. “Do you remember? I held the oath-flame, and you put your hand over it, and you said the words — freely given, freely given. You didn’t flinch. You were sixteen, and so proud you could hardly stand still.” His voice was very quiet, but the great round chamber carried it, every word. “And the next night I took you up on the wall at Emberwick, and gave you the taper, and let you light your first Ring-lamp on your own. Do you remember that? Your hands were shaking so, I thought you’d drop it over the parapet. And the wick caught, and the lamp went up gold all at once, and you laughed. Out loud. On the wall, at midnight. Half the Watch came running to see what was the matter.” He paused. “I’ve never heard a better sound in my life. Not before or since.” Varrick was looking at his own palm. “That boy,” said Ash, “is not dead. I’ve told you before. I never buried him. Pick up the lamp, lad. Not for her. Give it back to the girl, and come home. It isn’t too late. It’s never too late, while you can still hear me.” Wren held her breath. Up on the gallery, Mira’s fingers were crushing hers; Cinder was pressed against her legs, trembling. And Varrick hesitated. It was not a heartbeat this time. It was longer than that — much longer — so long that Wren began to believe, really to believe, that something was going to happen. His left hand had come up and closed over his scarred right palm, and was holding it, hard, the way you hold a burn. His head had bent. He stood there by the anvil, in the cold white light, and for the length of a long slow breath he looked like what he must once have been: a young man on a wall, at midnight, with a taper in his hand. Ash did not say anything more. He only waited, leaning on his one pole, as if he had all the time in the world, and meant to spend every bit of it here. Then his face closed. It closed the way a door closes in a big house, far away down a corridor: quietly, without a slam, but quite finally. He let go of his palm. He did not put the glove back on. “You talk too much, old man,” he said. “You always did.” And he struck. He did it fast, the way a snake does it. His bare hand swept the leaning pole away from the anvil, and the other pole out from under Ash’s arm, and the old man, who had only one good leg and nothing now to stand on, went down. He fell hard against the great anvil, and slid, and caught at the edge of it to save himself. Wren screamed. She did not know she was going to. She was already running — along the gallery, to where an iron stair went down the wall, and down it, three steps at a time, with Mira behind her clicking and Cinder ahead of them both, a grey streak with a spark for a tail. And Old Ash, on his knees at the anvil, reached up over the edge of it with one long hand, and his fingers closed on the lamp. He did not hold it to his chest. He did not hold it up against Varrick, or the hammers, or the dark. He turned on his knees, and he looked for Wren, and he found her — a small dark shape pelting down the iron stair — and he held the lamp out towards her, at the full length of his arm, the way he had once held out a cup of dreadful tea to a frightened chimney-sweep at his table, without asking anything at all. “Wren,” he said. “Here, child. Here. Take it.” And the lamp blazed. I do not know how to tell you how bright it was. Nobody who was there could ever tell it properly either. It was not like the white light of the glowstones. It did not glare, or dazzle, or make your eyes water. It was gold — deep, warm, living gold — and it filled the Great Forge from wall to wall in one breath, the way the sun fills a room when somebody throws back the curtains. And where it went, colour came back. The white floor was suddenly warm grey stone with veins of rust-red in it. The chains of the hammers were black iron with brown in the links. Mira’s dress was blue. Cinder’s coat was the grey of old ashes, warm and soft, and her tail-spark flared up like a struck match. And Old Ash’s coat, his old patched coat, which even by the lamp had only ever been a tired blue-grey — Ash’s coat was blue. A deep, clear, glad blue, like the sky must have been once, before the curse: Lamplighter blue, as it had been on the day it was new. Wren had not known it could be. The great hammer over the anvil shuddered on its chain, and stopped. Then all the hammers stopped, all round the shaft, one after another, high in the air, and hung there. And the shaft screamed. You will remember, if you have read the earlier parts of this story, that the Hollows make no sound, except one. Wren had heard it in Soot Lane, and on the Beacon, and in the Deeps. It came now out of the black shaft, out of the rolling dark itself, a long thin shriek that went on and on and set every tooth in her head aching. The dark in the shaft heaved and boiled and drew back from the gold like a hand from a stove. And all round the walls of the Great Forge, the glowstones began to crack. They cracked the way ice cracks on a pond in spring — with a sharp, singing crack here, and another there, and then a great many all at once, running across the walls in white lines. And out of every crack came a thread of grey-black cold, curling, loose, like smoke from a snuffed wick. The singing-stone in Wren’s pocket went from a keen to a shriek of its own. The white light of the walls flickered — and dimmed — and went out in patches, so that for the first time since they had come to Vaelport there were shadows, long and black and jumping. And the whole chamber shook. The grey smiths round the shaft had stopped too. They stood with their tongs hanging from their hands, and in the gold light Wren saw their faces change — not much; only a little; the way a sleeper’s face changes when somebody says his name. One of them, a big woman with a scarf over her hair, put up her hand and touched her own cheek, as though she had felt something there that she had forgotten about. “Up!” Old Ash’s voice rang across the forge, the way it must once have rung along the wall at Emberwick on a bad night. “Up, all of you! Out! Go up to the air!” And they went. They dropped their tongs and turned, slowly at first and then faster, stumbling, holding on to one another, and went streaming away into the tunnels towards the surface, a long grey line of them; and here and there among the grey, in the last of the gold, was a face that was not quite so grey as it had been. Varrick had flung up his bare arm across his eyes. He stood in the gold blaze with his face turned away from it, and he cried out, once, as if the light hurt him. Perhaps it did. For one moment, through the dazzle, Wren saw him look at the old man kneeling by the anvil with the lamp held out — just one look, and she never forgot it. Then he turned and ran. He ran into the mouth of a tunnel on the far side of the forge, where the glowstones had already gone dark, and the dark took him, and he was gone. Wren reached Ash. She did not remember crossing the floor. She only remembered falling on her knees beside him, and his arm coming round her, and the lamp warm and gold between them. Mira was there, clicking frantically, and Cinder was licking Ash’s face. “Hm,” said Ash. He was breathing hard, but his eyes were bright. “I thought I told you to stay on the quay.” “You did,” said Wren. “We didn’t.” A stone fell from the roof, somewhere behind them, as big as a cart, and burst on the floor like a dropped jar. “Up,” said Ash. “Up, child. My poles.” They got him to his feet between them. Wren found one pole and Mira found the other, and they put them in his hands. Ash hung the lamp on the brass hook at the end of the right-hand pole, the way he had carried lamps along the wall at Emberwick all his life, and lifted it high, and swung himself forward; and they went across the forge floor as fast as he could go, which was not very fast at all. Behind them the black shaft was pouring out its dark. It came up over the rim in a great slow wave and spread across the floor after them like a tide coming in over mud-flats, cold and grey and silent. Wherever it touched the gold of the lamp it shrank back; but there was so much of it, and it kept coming. The roof was falling now in earnest — not all at once, but in pieces, here and there, so that the whole chamber was full of the noise of it and of dust. Wren could not see for the dust. Nobody could. “Shut your eyes,” said Mira, “and hold his coat,” and shut her own, and clicked, and led them — round a fallen hammer-chain lying across the floor like a dead snake, past a split anvil, between two stones that came down in the time it took to say so. Ash went between the girls, swinging on his poles, with the lamp swaying gold on its hook above their heads. He did not hurry, because he could not. He breathed like a bellows with a hole in it. “I’ve walked the wall,” he said, between breaths, “in worse weather than this.” “You have not,” said Wren. “Hm,” said Ash. “No. Perhaps not.” “The door,” said Mira. “There’s a door ahead. I can hear the draught under it. Iron. And glass.” It stood in the wall at the top of three low steps: a great forge-door of iron bars with thick glass set between them, and beyond it a tunnel going steeply up. Ash had come in that way. It was the way out. They went through it. Mira first, then Wren, then Cinder; and Ash last of all, slow, on his poles. He turned in the doorway, and looked back once at the Great Forge, at the dark rolling towards him across the floor. He lifted the lamp off its hook. Then he let his poles fall, and took hold of the great door with his free hand, and swung it shut behind him; and leaned his back against it. The dark struck the other side. Wren felt it through the stone floor. The door jumped in its frame. Frost came racing across the glass in white feathers, and the iron bars groaned. Ash set his feet — his good one and his bad one — and leaned back, and held it. “Ash,” said Wren. “Ash, come on—“ “Go with them, girl,” said Ash, to Cinder. We’ll carry you. Mira — help me — we can carry him, he’s all bones, we can—“ The door jumped again. A crack ran across the glass behind his head. Old Ash held out the lamp to her. So he reached out and took her hands, gently, and put the lamp into them, and folded her fingers round it, and held them there a moment with his own, which were very warm. He looked at her.
